name: Christmas tree
desc: A Christmas tree is a decorated tree, usually an evergreen conifer such as a spruce, pine or fir, set up for the celebration of Christmas. The custom developed in Central Europe, particularly Germany and Livonia (now Estonia and Latvia), and was first recorded among German Lutherans in the 16th century; records indicate that a tree was placed in the Cathedral of Strasbourg in 1539. Trees were hung with apples, wafers, paper roses and confectionery and lit with candles, which electric lights have often replaced. In Britain the German-born Queen Charlotte introduced a tree in 1800, and the custom spread more widely after Queen Victoria's marriage to Prince Albert.

name: Santa Claus
desc: Santa Claus is a legendary figure originating in Western Christian culture who is said to bring gifts on the night of Christmas Eve. The figure derives from folklore surrounding Saint Nicholas, the 4th-century Greek bishop of Myra and patron saint of children, and from the Dutch Sinterklaas, whose legend settlers brought to 17th-century New Amsterdam; it also merged with the English Father Christmas. The name was first used in the United States press in 1773. The 1823 poem "A Visit from St. Nicholas", with its sleigh pulled by flying reindeer, laid the foundation for the modern image, which the cartoonist Thomas Nast helped to define in Harper's Weekly from 1863.

name: Sinterklaas
desc: Sinterklaas is a legendary figure of Dutch tradition based on Saint Nicholas (270–343), a Greek bishop of Myra in present-day Turkey and patron saint of children. He is depicted as an elderly, stately man with a long beard, in a red cape and mitre, who traditionally arrives by steamboat from Spain in mid-November and rides a white horse. Gifts are given on St. Nicholas' Eve, 5 December, in the Netherlands and on the morning of 6 December in Belgium, Luxembourg, western Germany and northern France. His helper Zwarte Piet ("Black Pete"), who first appeared in print in 1850, has been the subject of debate and protest since the 2010s over his blackface appearance.

name: Ded Moroz
desc: Ded Moroz, whose name is traditionally translated as Father Frost, is a legendary figure of East Slavic tradition similar to Father Christmas and Santa Claus. His origins predate Christianity as a Slavic personification of winter, and since the 19th century his legend has been shaped by literature, among it Aleksandr Ostrovsky's play The Snow Maiden. He is depicted with a long white beard, a heel-length fur coat and a magic stick, bringing presents at New Year with his granddaughter Snegurochka. In 1928 he was declared an ally of the priest and kulak, but traditions were revived after a letter published in Pravda in 1935, and he became the main symbol of the Soviet New Year's holiday.

name: Krampus
desc: The Krampus is a horned figure of Central and Eastern Alpine folklore who is said to accompany Saint Nicholas on visits to children on the night of 5 December, Krampusnacht, before the Feast of St. Nicholas. In the tradition Saint Nicholas rewards well-behaved children with small gifts, while Krampus, hairy and carrying chains and birch rods, punishes badly behaved ones. The origin of the figure is unclear: some folklorists have proposed pre-Christian roots, but historians generally consider this unlikely, as it is not attested until the 16th century. The tradition was prohibited in Austria under the Dollfuss regime and saw a popular resurgence towards the end of the 20th century.

name: Nativity of Jesus
desc: The Nativity of Jesus is the birth of Jesus as told in the Gospels of Matthew and Luke, the basis of the Christian holiday of Christmas. The two accounts agree that Jesus was born in Bethlehem in Judea in the reign of King Herod, to Mary, whose husband Joseph was descended from King David, and that the conception was divinely effected. Only Matthew has the wise men, the star of Bethlehem, the Massacre of the Innocents and the flight into Egypt; only Luke has the census of Quirinius and the adoration of the shepherds. The gospels state no date; reckoning from the death of Herod would place the birth between 6 and 4 BCE.

name: Nativity scene
desc: A nativity scene, also called a manger scene, crib or crèche, is a display, particularly during Christmastide, of figures representing the birth of Jesus. It shows Jesus, Mary and Joseph, usually with shepherds, angels, an ox and a donkey, and the Magi. The tradition comes from Italy: the first seasonal scene, which seems to have been enacted rather than sculpted, is attributed to Francis of Assisi, who is said to have staged it at Christmas 1223 in a cave near Greccio. Around 1290 Arnolfo di Cambio made a set of stone figures for Santa Maria Maggiore in Rome, and in the early modern period sculpted cribs, often exported from Italy, were set up in many churches and homes.

name: Christmas carol
desc: A Christmas carol is a song or hymn on the theme of Christmas, traditionally sung at Christmas or in the surrounding season. The first known Christmas hymns may be traced to 4th-century Rome, and by the 13th century popular Christmas songs in vernacular languages had developed in France, Germany and particularly Italy, under the influence of Francis of Assisi. The earliest English carols appear in a manuscript of 1426 by the Shropshire chaplain John Awdlay, who recorded twenty-five. Carols grew in popularity after the Protestant Reformation, when reformers such as Martin Luther promoted congregational singing, and printed collections of the 19th century widened their appeal.

name: Wassail
desc: Wassail is an English custom of Christmastide and the hot drink of mulled cider, ale or wine and spices that goes with it. The word was borrowed from the Old Norse salutation ves heill, 'be in good health'; its earliest record as a drinking formula is of around 1140, in Geoffrey of Monmouth, and by c. 1300 it also meant the drink itself. In the house-visiting wassail, traditionally on Twelfth Night (5 January), people go from door to door singing and offering a drink from the wassail bowl in exchange for gifts, a practice largely displaced by carol singing. In the orchard-visiting wassail of England's cider-producing regions, people sing to the trees to promote a good harvest.

name: Winter solstice
desc: The winter solstice is the moment when one of Earth's poles reaches its maximum tilt away from the Sun, giving that hemisphere its shortest day and longest night of the year. In the Northern Hemisphere it falls on 21 or 22 December and in the Southern on 20 or 21 June. Since prehistory it has been marked by festivals and rites in many cultures, as the point when daylight begins to increase again; monuments such as Newgrange in Ireland and Stonehenge in England are aligned with its sunrise or sunset. In the ancient Roman calendar the solstice was dated to 25 December, which the emperor Aurelian made the festival of the birthday of Sol Invictus in 274 CE.

name: Lohri
desc: Lohri is a midwinter folk and harvest festival of the Punjab region of India and Pakistan and other parts of northern India, marking the passing of the winter solstice and the end of winter. It falls on the night before Maghi (Makar Sankranti), commonly 13 January, and is celebrated by lighting bonfires, eating festive foods such as jaggery and gajak, singing, and dancing the bhangra and giddha. Many of its songs tell the legend of Dulla Bhatti, set in the reign of the Mughal emperor Akbar and regarded in Punjab as a hero for rescuing girls from being sold in slave markets. European visitors mentioned the festival at the Lahore court of Maharaja Ranjit Singh in the 1830s.

name: Makar Sankranti
desc: Makar Sankranti is a Hindu observance and midwinter harvest festival in India and Nepal, typically celebrated on 14 January (15 January in a leap year). It marks the transition of the Sun from the zodiac sign of Sagittarius to Capricorn (makara), which coincides with its movement from south to north, and is dedicated to the solar deity Surya. The festival is known by many regional names, among them Pongal in Tamil Nadu, Magh Bihu in Assam and Uttarayana in Gujarat. It is observed with fairs, kite flying, bonfires and feasts, and many observers bathe in sacred rivers or lakes in thanks to the Sun. Every twelve years it is observed with the Kumbha Mela, a mass pilgrimage.
